notes: Long procedural history but full Court of Appeal judgment on CPR security-for-costs principles and automatic stay under PD 51 para 19.

enrichment.short_title: Conditional stay of County Court appeal pending costs payment set aside where litigant in person lacked good faith finding
key_facts: Mr Ali sued his former solicitor Mr Hudson for negligence relating to a failed restaurant sale claim that had already been struck out in the High Court.
District Judge Hasan struck out Mr Ali's claim in July 1998 and ordered costs of about £14,592; Mr Ali lodged a timely appeal but the court did not list it until May 2002.

Judge Green ordered the appeal stayed pending payment of taxed costs plus interest; Leveson J varied this to payment of £1,750 into court, but no inquiry was made into Mr Ali's means (he was on income support).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal with permission against Leveson J's order partially allowing Mr Ali's appeal from Judge Green's conditional stay of a County Court appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Leveson J's order set aside; automatic stay under CPR PD 51 para 19(1) lifted; Mr Ali permitted to pursue his appeal against the strike-out with directions for properly formulated grounds.
enrichment.ratio: Before imposing a conditional stay or payment into court as security for costs outside CPR r 25.13, the court must apply Olatawura principles with great caution: such orders should ordinarily be made only where a party regularly flouts procedure or shows want of good faith, and not simply because of delay or a weak case; requiring payment of costs subject to appeal as a condition of proceeding effectively stifles access to court and was inappropriate here.
legal_issues: Whether Judge Green and Leveson J had jurisdiction under CPR Pt 3 to order a stay conditional on payment of costs
Whether Mr Ali's delay in prosecuting his appeal amounted to abuse of process or lack of good faith
Whether a condition requiring payment of costs under appeal could lawfully or fairly be imposed on an impecunious litigant in person
Whether the automatic stay under CPR PD 51 para 19(1) should be lifted

notes: Clear costs appeal on CPR Pt 36 and Pt 44 principles in Patents County Court proceedings.

enrichment.short_title: Patent infringement costs varied after claimant failed to beat defendant's Part 36 offer on prior use
key_facts: Kavanagh Balloons sued Cameron Balloons for infringement of a European patent relating to hot air balloon vent systems.
Prior use invalidated several claims but claims 3 and 11 were held valid and infringed by the Smart Vent product.

Cameron Balloons made a Part 36 offer on 22 June 2001 that largely anticipated the trial outcome; Judge Fysh QC ordered Kavanagh to pay 60% of defendant's post-offer costs and made no order for the pre-offer period.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against costs orders made by HHJ Fysh QC in the Patents County Court following trial on patent validity and infringement.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; claimant ordered to pay 75% of defendant's costs for the pre-offer period and all defendant's post-offer costs (save costs relating to named witnesses covered by paragraph 10 of the judge's order); increased interim payment of £55,000 ordered.
enrichment.ratio: Where distinct issues are clearly separable, costs should be allocated issue-by-issue; CPR r 36.20(2) requires full post-offer costs unless injustice is shown, and the mere difficulty of prior use cases turning on witness evidence does not make it unjust to apply the Part 36 consequences when detailed particulars had been served before the offer.
legal_issues: Whether the judge erred in making no order as to costs before expiry of the Part 36 offer period
Whether it was unjust under CPR r 36.20(2) to order full post-offer costs because prior use evidence depended on witness box testimony
Whether partial success on claim 3 justified departing from the normal Part 36 costs consequences

notes: Divisional Court appeal under Solicitors Act 1974 s 49 quashing SDT findings on shipping recovery litigation conduct.

enrichment.short_title: Solicitor's disciplinary findings quashed where tribunal focused on wrong client-identification issue
key_facts: Mr Stokes, a shipping solicitor, acted for cargo underwriter Nordstern through recovery agents IRS and solicitor Mr Bentley in proceedings against Internav for misapplied collision recovery funds.

The Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal found conduct unbefitting in failing to communicate directly with Nordstern and acting without proper authority, fining him £5,000; dishonesty allegations were abandoned days before the hearing.

The Tribunal wrongly treated Bentley's admissions as evidence against Stokes, stated Bentley gave oral evidence when he did not, and did not consider a key IRS letter to Gustav Ziegler showing the instruction chain.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Divisional Court under section 49 of the Solicitors Act 1974 against findings of the Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Tribunal findings quashed; Law Society ordered to pay appellant's appeal costs and one third of costs below.
enrichment.ratio: Disciplinary findings were fatally flawed because the Tribunal misidentified the issue as whether Nordstern was the solicitor's client rather than whether acting through IRS/Bentley with Nordstern's written authority and reporting up the agency chain was professionally acceptable in shipping recovery practice; Bentley's admissions and Drake J's findings against Bentley could not prove misconduct by Stokes.
legal_issues: Whether Nordstern was Mr Stokes's client or whether communication through IRS and Gustav Ziegler was sufficient
Whether the Tribunal's reasoning was vitiated by procedural and evidential errors
Whether shipping market practice permitted a solicitor to take instructions through recovery agents
What costs order should follow quashing of the disciplinary findings

notes: Appeal on discretion to lift stay in long-running mesne profits claim; appeal dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: Stay lifted in mesne profits claim despite delay where no prejudice and amendment to plead trespass possible
key_facts: Mr King claimed mesne profits against Miss Job-Tyoran for occupying part of premises he owned, following related possession proceedings against her father.
Proceedings begun in 1995 were stayed in April 2000 pending outcome of the father's possession actions; the stay was not lifted until September 2003 after delays by the claimant.
Judge Wakefield lifted the stay and dismissed the defendant's strike-out application, finding no prejudice and that the claim might be amended to plead trespass.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the High Court with permission against HHJ Wakefield's order lifting a stay and refusing to strike out a mesne profits claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; case management conference to be relisted.
enrichment.ratio: Failure to provide a fully satisfactory explanation for delay in applying to lift a stay does not of itself make the judge's exercise of discretion unlawful or irrational; where there is no prejudice, a fair trial remains possible, and the claim has a real prospect of success if amended to plead trespass, refusing to lift the stay would be a disproportionate response.
legal_issues: Whether the claimant's delay in applying to lift the stay justified refusing reinstatement
Whether the judge should have struck out the claim as having no real prospect of success
Whether alleged limitation prejudice or changed circumstances amounted to prejudice warranting maintaining the stay
Whether observations that the claim was unlikely to succeed on current pleading equated to a strike-out finding

notes: Boundary construction and proprietary estoppel appeal; claimants succeeded on construction but appeal dismissed on estoppel.

enrichment.short_title: Gabion retaining wall held to encroach on neighbour's land but proprietary estoppel barred removal
key_facts: Neighbours on the Rosebank estate at Ramsbottom disputed whether the boundary on a 1994 transfer plan was 600mm from the rear of an old mill retaining wall on Plot 7 or on the Plot 8 side.
The Kenwards installed gabion retaining walls partly on the Kuligowskis' Plot 8 before and after the Kuligowskis purchased their plot.

The Court of Appeal held the boundary was 600mm from the rear of the wall on the Plot 7 side, so lower gabion rows encroached, but proprietary estoppel based on Rosebank developer Mr Carswell's consent prevented relief.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against a County Court decision dismissing trespass and nuisance claims and declaring the boundary along the front of the bottom gabion.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; claimants to pay 80% of defendants' costs; boundary construction decided in claimants' favour but proprietary estoppel defeated their claim for removal or damages in lieu.
enrichment.ratio: Construction of a conveyancing plan defining a boundary by measurement from a retaining wall is a question of law on which expert opinion is inadmissible if the plan is clear; where the landowner encouraged installation of encroaching structures and the occupier relied to their detriment, proprietary estoppel may defeat a trespass claim even if the boundary line favours the claimant.
legal_issues: Construction of the 1994 transfer plan and meaning of 'rear of retaining wall'
Whether expert evidence on plan interpretation was admissible
Whether proprietary estoppel arose from Mr Carswell's consent to gabion placement
Whether a quia timet nuisance claim required proof of imminent danger of substantial damage

notes: School's appeal against SEND Tribunal disability discrimination finding on pastoral support for autistic pupil; appeal dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: School disability discrimination upheld for failure to provide adequate pastoral support to autistic pupil

statutes_considered.title: Special Educational Needs and Disability Act 2001
Education (Pupil Exclusions and Appeals) (Maintained Schools) (England) Regulations 2002

key_facts: IC, a pupil with autistic spectrum disorder at McA Catholic High School, experienced deteriorating behaviour, bullying incidents and a serious fixed-term exclusion after a dining hall altercation in November 2002.
Parents complained to the SEND Tribunal that the school failed to make reasonable adjustments, including pastoral support during unstructured times and on transition from Year 7 to Year 8.
The Tribunal upheld discrimination solely on lack of personal guidance and support within the pastoral system and ordered an action plan including mentoring and buddy arrangements.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the High Court by the school against a Special Educational Needs and Disability Tribunal decision allowing parents' disability discrimination claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Tribunal decision upheld; school ordered to pay Tribunal costs summarily assessed at £3,564.
enrichment.ratio: In education disability discrimination under section 28B(1)(a), the proper comparator is a non-disabled pupil who has not behaved badly, not a non-disabled pupil exhibiting the same behaviour; fixed-term exclusion did not oust Tribunal jurisdiction, and failure to plan pastoral support for an autistic pupil's transition and unstructured periods could amount to less favourable treatment related to disability under section 28C.
legal_issues: Whether the Tribunal had jurisdiction given the pupil's fixed-term exclusion
Who was the correct comparator for less favourable treatment under section 28B(1)(a)
Whether the Tribunal erred in finding inadequate pastoral support amounted to discrimination
Whether the Tribunal acted unfairly in failing to put the pastoral support issue to the head teacher

notes: Judicial review on Article 5.4 review rights for discretionary life prisoner transferred to hospital under MHA; claim dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: Discretionary lifer in hospital has no Article 5.4 right to single combined MHRT and Parole Board hearing
key_facts: P is a discretionary life prisoner whose 10-year tariff expired; he was transferred to Broadmoor under section 47 MHA with a section 49 restriction direction in 1994.

Under domestic law following Hickey, P had no right to apply to the Parole Board until a mental health review tribunal notified the Home Secretary under section 74 that he would be entitled to discharge.
P argued Article 5.4 required a single tribunal to review all bases of detention and that consecutive MHRT and DLP hearings caused unlawful delay.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review of the lawfulness of the statutory scheme governing review of detention of a discretionary life prisoner transferred to hospital under the Mental Health Act 1983.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; permission to appeal refused; Stanley Burnton J held consecutive MHRT and Parole Board hearings are not mandatorily incompatible with Article 5.4.
enrichment.ratio: Article 5.4 does not require a single court to determine lawfulness of detention under every applicable sub-paragraph of Article 5.1; where a patient remains lawfully detained under the MHA, he is not entitled under Article 5.4 to review of continued detention as a lifer until discharge from mental health detention is warranted, and consecutive hearings do not necessarily breach the requirement of a speedy decision.
legal_issues: Whether section 34 CJA must be read compatibly with the Convention to give all tariff-expired discretionary lifers a Parole Board review right
Whether Article 5.4 requires joint mental health review tribunal and Discretionary Lifer Panel hearings
Whether consecutive hearings inevitably cause delay incompatible with Article 5.4
Whether continued restriction directions where a patient presents risk only to himself violate Article 5

notes: CCRC reference; unsafe conviction due to inadequate joint enterprise direction to jury.

enrichment.short_title: Robbery conviction unsafe after judge wrongly answered jury question on joint enterprise
key_facts: Howard was convicted by an 11-1 majority of robbery after Martin Mayes was attacked and bags stolen on the Hayway in Rushden on 23 December 2000.
The appellant admitted getting out of the robbers' car but claimed he only urinated nearby and did not participate in the robbery.

The jury asked whether the defendant could be guilty if he knowingly went with others knowing they would commit the offence; the judge answered simply 'Yes', without explaining required participation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction following reference by the Criminal Cases Review Commission after the appellant did not appeal at the time on counsel's advice.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; conviction quashed as unsafe.
enrichment.ratio: A conviction for robbery by joint enterprise is unsafe where the judge failed adequately to direct the jury that mere presence and knowledge that others intended to commit robbery is insufficient without participation by encouragement or otherwise; answering the jury's specific question with a bare 'yes' was a material misdirection.
legal_issues: Whether the summing-up adequately explained joint enterprise liability for robbery
Whether the judge's answer to the jury's written question was a misdirection
Whether the conviction was nevertheless safe because the jury must have been sure the appellant participated

notes: Leading analysis of section 5 CACA interim powers including local authority accommodation and electronic tagging.

enrichment.short_title: Hague Convention section 5 interim powers include directing local authority accommodation for abducted child
key_facts: An American father brought Hague Convention proceedings after an Irish mother wrongfully retained their nine-year-old child in England following prior abduction from California.

The child was temporarily placed in foster care via police protection; the court considered whether section 5 CACA authorised directing a local authority to accommodate the child pending the return application.
The mother had evaded detection for over four years using assumed names, creating high flight risk where standard passport and port alert measures might be insufficient.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory hearing in High Court Hague Convention proceedings to determine the scope of interim powers under section 5 of the Child Abduction and Custody Act 1985.
enrichment.outcome: Court held section 5 CACA permits interim directions requiring a local authority to arrange temporary accommodation for a child in appropriate high-risk abduction cases, and may include electronic tagging of a parent with consent; substantive Hague hearing adjourned.
enrichment.ratio: Section 5 CACA implements Article 7(b) of the Hague Convention and is a self-contained code broad enough to authorise provisional measures including inviting a local authority to arrange interim care, without treating the child as looked after under the Children Act 1989; such directions should be used only when other protective measures are inadequate.
legal_issues: Whether section 5 CACA authorises directing a local authority to accommodate a child pending Hague proceedings
Whether the Children Act 1989 precludes use of local authority accommodation in Hague cases
How section 5 interacts with Article 16 and section 9 moratorium on merits decisions
Whether electronic tagging may be ordered as an interim protective measure under section 5

notes: Substantial liability judgment on breach of fiduciary duty, confidential information misuse and enforceability of post-termination restraints.

enrichment.short_title: Sales director liable for passing customer database to competitor and breaching non-solicitation covenant
key_facts: Andrew Brown, sales director of LC Services Ltd (laboratory equipment maintenance), resigned on 27 March 2003 to join Kinesis Solutions Ltd, a new competitor associated with parts supplier Kinesis Ltd.

Before and after leaving, Brown transferred LCS's ACT! customer database to Kinesis's Goldmine system, removed renewal lead files, failed to send renewal quotations, and solicited LCS customers including Britvic, Dermal and Croda Colloids.
KSL knowingly participated in Brown's breaches; the court found Brown deliberately misled LCS about joining a competitor to avoid garden leave.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court trial of liability issues in claims for breach of contract, breach of fiduciary duty, misuse of confidential information, and enforcement of post-termination restrictive covenants.
enrichment.outcome: LCS succeeded on liability; Brown and KSL held liable for breach of contract, fiduciary duty and misuse of confidential information; clause 17.2 non-solicitation covenant held enforceable; damages/account of profits to be assessed.
enrichment.ratio: A director owes a duty of fidelity not to compete or solicit customers for a rival during employment; post-termination non-solicitation of customers with whom the employee dealt in the last 12 months is enforceable to protect legitimate customer connections built for the employer, and wholesale transfer of the employer's customer database to a competitor is misuse of confidential information even where some data is obtainable elsewhere.
legal_issues: Whether Brown breached fiduciary and contractual duties by preparing to join KSL while still employed
Whether LCS's ACT! database and red lever-arch renewal files were confidential information misused by the defendants
Whether clause 17.2 non-solicitation and non-interference covenants were reasonable and enforceable
Whether KSL was liable for inducing or participating in Brown's breaches
